 Home Alert Medicare open enrollment requires careful review of coverage Medicare open enrollment requires careful review of coverage
 Sun, November 1, 2026 by Staff Report 
 SHARE NOW 
 Paperwork. Close-up part of group of people brainstorming and holding documents and digital tablet while sitting at office 
 As Medicare open enrollment continues, older Americans are being urged to carefully review their health and prescription drug coverage rather than automatically renewing the plans they had the previous year. The enrollment process has become increasingly complicated, particularly for seniors who are expected to navigate changing insurance options and technology.
 Sometimes even seemingly simple tasks, such as scanning QR codes or using voice assistants to access information, can create obstacles for older adults. Many seniors experience vision and hearing difficulties, making technology-based interactions even more frustrating. Michael Day of Michael G. Day Law and Associates in Hagerstown said, “We have people who have hearing issues that get worse as they get older. They have vision issues that get worse as they get older.”
 He said his law practice and trust company have moved away from automated answering systems because clients benefit from speaking directly with someone who can explain information in a way they understand.
 “We don’t use automated answering. Senior citizens don’t like it,” Day said. “You need to have people who are interfacing with them at their level of understanding of technology, which is one-on-one.” Medicare recipients should seek assistance from knowledgeable professionals rather than trying to navigate complicated coverage decisions on their own.
 “I think self-help in this area, for most folks, is not a good idea,” Day said. “I don’t think the information is designed for you to be able to fully understand it.” One of the biggest distinctions consumers need to understand is the difference between Medicare Advantage plans and traditional Medicare combined with a Medicare supplement.
 Medicare Advantage plans are offered through private insurance companies and can restrict which doctors and medical facilities patients can access. Traditional Medicare combined with a supplemental policy generally offers greater flexibility when seeking care from providers who accept Medicare.
 Day questioned the use of the word advantage in describing the private insurance plans. “I think anytime the government or an insurance company tells you it’s an advantage, you should be circumspect right off the gate,” he said. He explained that Medicare Advantage patients are relying on insurance companies to determine which services are covered and which providers are included in their networks.
 “You’re opting out of Medicare. You’re now relying on insurance folks to provide you the care that you need as a person over 65,” Day said.
 He described clients who encountered difficulties obtaining referrals to specialized medical facilities because those facilities were not included in their Medicare Advantage networks.
 In one case, a Pennsylvania resident was referred to Hershey for a particular procedure but was unable to access the facility through their Medicare Advantage network. Another client with a complicated medical diagnosis was referred to the Cleveland Clinic, but the client’s Medicare Advantage coverage presented obstacles to receiving care there.
 Day said traditional Medicare combined with a Medicare supplement generally provides greater freedom to seek treatment at facilities across the country that accept Medicare. “As people age, they want to be able to access those services,” he said. Consumers shouldn’t necessarily assume Medicare Advantage provides the same coverage and flexibility as traditional Medicare combined with a supplemental policy.
 “It’s not the equivalent of Medicare Part A and Part B and a Medicare supplement,” Day said. “But when people hear that, they think it is comparable, and it’s not.”
 Medicare Advantage plans and Medicare Part D prescription drug plans serve different purposes, even though many Medicare Advantage plans incorporate prescription coverage.
 Medicare Advantage provides medical coverage, while Part D covers prescription medications. During open enrollment, consumers need to review both aspects of their coverage to make sure their plans will continue meeting their needs in the coming year.
 Day said prescription coverage can change from year to year, even when someone is satisfied with the medical portion of their plan.
 Consumers need to make sure their medications remain covered and consider switching plans if necessary. He warned that failing to review prescription coverage can have significant financial consequences, particularly when expensive medications are involved.
 Day cited an example of a medication costing $600 per month that was not covered by a particular plan.
 Those expenses would not count toward the annual out-of-pocket limit for covered Part D medications, potentially leaving patients responsible for the cost throughout the year. Day said he regularly encounters people who simply allow their existing coverage to renew without examining the changes for the upcoming year. Do people ever give up trying to understand all this and opt to not make any changes?
 “All the time,” Day said. “They just can’t do it because there’s huge financial risk in the failure to do that.”
 He warned that consumers who fail to review their plans could find themselves unable to access preferred physicians, obtain certain procedures or afford necessary medications.Day encouraged Medicare recipients to take the time to examine their coverage every year and seek help when they do not understand their options.
